title: Respiratory: Asthma/Lung Disease Flares, Chest Tubes, Pulmonary Embolism

questions.stem: A client having an asthma flare was wheezing loudly. Now the wheezing has stopped and the chest is quiet. What does this mean?

options.text: Almost no air is moving: an emergency

questions.explanation: B is correct: when wheezing suddenly stops and the chest goes quiet, almost no air is moving, which is an emergency. A and C wrongly read it as better. D ignores the danger.

questions.stem: Which findings are expected during an asthma or chronic lung disease flare? Select all that apply.

options.text: Using neck and chest muscles to breathe

questions.explanation: A, B, and C are correct: wheezing, extra neck and chest muscle use, and being unable to finish a sentence are taught flare signs. D and E describe comfortable breathing.

questions.stem: What is the usual oxygen saturation target for a client with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, per the provider's order?
questions.explanation: B is correct: the usual target is about 88 to 92%, per the provider's order. A is too low. C is higher than the usual target in this disease. D isn't possible.

questions.stem: A client with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is in respiratory distress. Which action is correct?

options.text: Give oxygen and sit the client upright
Wait for a blood gas before giving oxygen

questions.explanation: B is correct: sit the client upright and give oxygen; never withhold oxygen in respiratory distress. A and D withhold oxygen. C, lying flat, doesn't help breathing.

questions.stem: The water-seal chamber of a chest tube rises and falls with each breath. What does this mean?
questions.explanation: B is correct: rising and falling with each breath, called tidaling, is expected. A, constant bubbling, would be a leak. C and D aren't what tidaling means.

questions.stem: The water-seal chamber bubbles constantly. What is the nurse's first action?

options.text: Check the connections from the client to the unit
Clamp the tube for an hour
Raise the unit above the chest

questions.explanation: B is correct: constant bubbling in the water seal means an air leak, so check the connections and notify the provider. A calls it normal. C, clamping, isn't the taught step. D is wrong because the unit stays below the chest.

questions.stem: Which actions are correct for a client with a chest tube? Select all that apply.

options.text: Keep the drainage unit below the chest
Keep the tubing free of kinks
Expect gentle bubbling in the suction chamber
Report constant bubbling in the water seal
Hang the unit on the bed rail above the chest

questions.explanation: A, B, C, and D are correct: keep the unit below the chest and the tubing free of kinks; gentle suction-chamber bubbling is normal; constant water-seal bubbling is a leak to report. E is wrong because the unit must stay below the chest.

questions.stem: A chest tube accidentally pulls out of the client's chest. What is the first action?

options.text: Cover the site with a sterile dressing taped on three sides

questions.explanation: B is correct: a dressing taped on three sides lets air escape but not get sucked in; then notify the provider. A, never try to reinsert it. C doesn't cover the open site. D delays covering the site.

questions.stem: Which findings suggest a pulmonary embolism? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: A, B, C, and D are correct: these are the taught signs of a clot blocking blood flow in the lungs. E is gradual, not the sudden picture of an embolism.

questions.stem: A client suddenly becomes short of breath with sharp chest pain. A pulmonary embolism is suspected. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Stay, sit the client up, give oxygen, and call the rapid response team
Lay the client flat and recheck in an hour

questions.explanation: B is correct: stay with the client, sit them up, give oxygen, and call the rapid response team. A leaves the client. C delays care. D isn't taught and adds strain.
